say.text: Last stretch. You will build the one-page TOF summary yourself, one piece at a time, with no teaching first.
Pick the line you would want on your own revision sheet.
Piece 1: the anatomy. Which set lists the four components of classic TOF?

choices.label: VSD, overriding aorta, pulmonary stenosis, ASD
VSD, overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction, RVH
VSD, overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction, LVH

say.text: Start from one septal defect and ask which ventricle faces the obstruction. Which ventricle would thicken?
ASD is tempting: it is a familiar shunt that sits beside cyanotic heart disease, so it slips into the list.
But ASD and PDA only may accompany TOF; the four listed by StatPearls and CDC include no ASD, PDA or LVH.
The fourth component is right ventricular hypertrophy.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pause here: the four come from one malaligned septum, not from a list of shunts.

say.text: Yes: a large, anteriorly malaligned VSD, an overriding aorta, infundibular RVOT obstruction and right ventricular hypertrophy.
ASD and PDA may accompany TOF but are not among the four. PYQs have keyed PDA, ASD and LVH as not part of TOF.
LVH is tempting because 'ventricular hypertrophy' was stored without a side.
The ventricle that thickens is the one pushing against the narrowed outflow: right ventricular hypertrophy, secondary to chronic systemic pressures. LVH is not among the four.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pause here: the thick ventricle in TOF is the right one.

say.text: Piece 2: the chain. Which sequence puts cause before effect?

choices.label: Large VSD floods the lungs, then left ventricle overloads, then LVH
Malaligned VSD, then infundibular narrowing, then RV pressure load, then RVH
RV muscle thickens first, which then narrows the infundibulum, then the VSD

say.text: A shunt that floods the lungs is tempting because most holes in the septum do that.
In TOF, with significant RVOT obstruction most blood shunts toward the aorta, bypassing the pulmonary bed. The ventricle that hypertrophies is the right one.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so recheck the direction of flow: past the obstruction, towards the aorta.

say.text: Right. The malaligned septum comes with infundibular obstruction, and the right ventricle then hypertrophies, secondary to chronic systemic pressures.
This reverses cause and effect. A thick muscle looks like a primary lesion, so it is tempting to start there.
RVH is secondary to chronic systemic pressures, so it sits at the end of the chain, after the infundibular obstruction.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so recheck: the hypertrophy is a consequence, not the start.

say.text: Piece 3: ECG and film. Which pair belongs on the summary?

choices.label: Right axis deviation with prominent R in V1; oligaemic lung fields
Left axis deviation with LVH pattern; plethoric lung fields
Right axis deviation with RVH pattern; increased pulmonary vascular markings

say.text: Yes. The ECG shows right axis deviation and prominent R or qR waves in V1. Blood bypasses the lungs, so the film can show pulmonary oligaemia.
StatPearls describes a normal-size heart silhouette; the boot shape is a classic that may be seen.
Left-sided changes are tempting if hypertrophy is stored without a side and a VSD is expected to flood the lungs.
The load is on the right ventricle, so the ECG is right-sided, and with RVOT obstruction most blood bypasses the pulmonary bed.
The ECG half is right, which makes the second half tempting: a VSD sounds like extra lung flow.
But the blood is shunted toward the aorta, so the film can show decreased pulmonary vascular markings, not increased ones.
Piece 4: the test ladder. Which line is right?

choices.label: Catheterisation is the gold standard; echo is only a screen
MRI is first-line diagnosis; echo is kept for follow-up
Echo diagnoses; CT shows morphology; MRI adds function without radiation

say.text: Catheterisation sounds like the invasive, definitive test, so it is tempting as gold standard.
The source names the echocardiogram as the gold standard for diagnosis; it allows direct visualisation of the abnormal anatomy.
MRI is tempting because it gives rich detail without radiation, so it feels like a better first test.
But echocardiography remains the primary modality for diagnosis. MRI adds anatomical detail plus functional information.
Right. Echocardiography is the gold standard and primary diagnostic modality; contrast-enhanced CT shows the complex morphology; MRI gives anatomy and function without ionising radiation.
Piece 5: a tet spell. Which order of steps goes on the summary?

choices.label: Phenylephrine, then morphine, then knee-chest position and oxygen
Oxygen, then IV furosemide, then digoxin
Knee-chest position and oxygen, then IV fluids, then beta-blocker or phenylephrine

say.text: Think of what you can do in seconds with no drug, then volume, then drugs. Which measures need no cannula?
Starting with the strongest drug is tempting because a blue, limp child looks like an emergency for drugs.
But the list begins with the bedside levers, knee-chest positioning and oxygen. Morphine is a sedative given during a spell.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is worth a second look: bedside levers come before drugs.

say.text: A diuretic and digoxin are tempting if a breathless child is read as heart failure.
Each spell measure acts on systemic resistance, pulmonary vasodilation or RV filling, such as fluid boluses to improve RV filling. A diuretic empties the RV further.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is worth a second look: a spell is about resistance and filling, not congestion.

say.text: Yes. Spells need a rapid, aggressive approach, and the list runs: knee-chest to raise systemic resistance, oxygen for pulmonary vasodilation, IV fluid boluses for RV filling.
Then IV beta-blockers slow the heart rate, and IV phenylephrine raises systemic afterload.
Piece 6: levers. Which two measures share the same aim?
Aim: raise systemic afterload.
Pairing them is tempting if positioning is thought to help the lungs directly.

Oxygen causes pulmonary vasodilation, but knee-chest positioning acts on the systemic side, to increase systemic vascular resistance. If resistance across the RVOT is less than systemic resistance, the child is minimally cyanotic or acyanotic.
Heart-failure drugs are tempting for a child who looks breathless and limp.
The spell measures aim at systemic resistance, pulmonary vasodilation and RV filling. Neither a diuretic nor digoxin is among them.
Yes. Knee-chest positioning increases systemic vascular resistance, and IV phenylephrine increases systemic afterload. Oxygen works on the pulmonary side.
Piece 7: after repair. Which line belongs on the summary?

choices.label: Residual VSD is the commonest reoperation reason; late risks continue
Pulmonary insufficiency is the commonest reoperation reason; late risks end
Pulmonary insufficiency is the commonest reoperation reason; late risks continue

say.text: Residual VSD is tempting if surgery is imagined to leave the old defects behind.
The repair itself changes the RVOT: reconstruction produces pulmonary regurgitation, and pulmonary insufficiency is the most common indication for reoperation.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask what the operation itself changed: the RVOT.

say.text: The second half is tempting because repair feels like cure.
But arrhythmias, including ventricular tachycardia, can occur after repair, and patients with TOF, repaired or unrepaired, are at risk of endocarditis.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note the qualifier: repaired or unrepaired.

say.text: Yes. Pulmonary regurgitation results from reconstruction of the RVOT, and pulmonary insufficiency is the most common indication for reoperation.
Ventricular tachycardia can occur after repair, and patients with TOF, repaired or unrepaired, are at risk of endocarditis.
Piece 8: a number for the sheet. About what share of adults with repaired TOF can have ventricular arrhythmias?
Yes: 40–50% of adults with repaired TOF can have ventricular arrhythmias. Sudden death risk is 6–9% 30 years after the procedure.
A good repair feels like it should end the risk, which makes this tempting.
Yet 40–50% of adults with repaired TOF can have ventricular arrhythmias.
Your sheet: one malaligned septum gives the four; RV load gives right-sided ECG and oligaemic lungs; echo diagnoses; spells are managed by resistance and filling levers.
Without surgery, hypoxic spells (68%) lead the causes of death.

cards.a: Large anteriorly malaligned VSD, overriding aorta, infundibular RVOT obstruction, RV hypertrophy. ASD and PDA may accompany but are not among the four.

cards.q: Why does RVH occur in TOF?
cards.a: It is secondary to chronic systemic pressures, after infundibular obstruction.
Right axis deviation, prominent R or qR in V1; decreased pulmonary vascular markings.
Echocardiography; contrast CT shows complex morphology, MRI adds function without ionising radiation.
Knee-chest raises systemic resistance, oxygen dilates the pulmonary bed, fluids improve RV filling, beta-blockers slow rate, phenylephrine raises afterload.
Pulmonary insufficiency, from RVOT reconstruction; arrhythmia and endocarditis risks remain.
